name: Hassan Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without employer or political ties. This interview is confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a carpentry crew on building sites, from setting out walls to fixing the last door that will not close. I have a trade certificate and can spot a twisted frame before anyone reaches for a screen. My partner and I have two children in school, a mortgage and more than six months put aside; the wage is good, and there are other sites nearby. I like making apprentices accurate, though I am tired of plans changing after the timber arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI Plateau leaves us much where we are: carpenters still measure and fit the timber. The office may print forms faster, but no form fixes a crooked opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be glad to keep the same work and pay while the children are in school. We have savings, yet I still feel the mortgage each month, so I do not take another steady year for granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading the carpentry crew and checking drawings against the actual wall before we cut. In the first year after this mild change, I'd keep our mortgage payment schedule and add the same extra amount from each wage to savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about our income. I know a site can close for ordinary reasons, but I could find another carpentry crew nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still check by hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a tape to the opening and mark the true width on the drawing before the doors arrive. That one check saves half a day's rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the household savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I agreed the savings top-up stays while my higher wage lasts. School costs are coming, so we keep the household ledger plain.

say: **AI Plateau** would leave carpentry fitting and site checks largely in skilled hands.
I would remind the crew that a quicker **office form** cannot straighten a crooked opening.
think: I expect my **higher wage** to continue while the children are still at school.
Our **mortgage** remains a monthly pressure even with more than six months saved.
do: **Keep** leading carpentry work and measuring openings before cutting timber.
**Add** a fixed extra amount from each wage payment to household savings.
feel: I feel **calm** about our income, with ordinary site and mortgage worries still present.
S0.quote: The office may print forms faster, but no form fixes a crooked opening.
fieldNote: He trusts a **tape measure** and skilled judgment more than office forms.
Strong savings and **nearby site work** make the mortgage manageable despite ordinary construction uncertainty.

steps.text: Keep leading carpentry crew and checking openings before cutting timber
Add the agreed extra amount from each wage to household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption changes the planner and buyer first, while our hands still build the walls. The crew should see revised drawings before a machine's order reaches the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faster planning could mean fewer people in the office, then more rushed work pushed onto us. I do not use AI tools, and I would rather have a named person responsible for a wrong timber order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask our union site representative to bring drawing changes to the next safety meeting. In the first year, I'd keep fitting and supervising, and ask for printed revisions signed by a responsible site planner before we cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the pressure could rise even if my own hours and wage stay intact. I do not want a computer's mistake pinned on an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentice would get the old and new drawing side by side, then we would measure the actual wall. I would stop a cut if the dimension still did not agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should own a revised drawing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the planner's name and revision date on the sheet. If nobody owns the drawing, the carpenter becomes the last person blamed.

say: **Steady Disruption** would change buying and planning before hands-on carpentry on site.
I would insist on **signed drawings** before the crew cuts timber for altered walls.
think: My own **hours** appear safe, but faster planning could increase pressure on the crew.
I privately fear an **apprentice** might carry blame for an office ordering mistake.
do: **Raise** drawing changes with the union site representative at the next safety meeting.
**Keep** supervising fitting work and require dated, signed drawing revisions before cuts.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about site pressure, though our household pay still looks secure.
S1.quote: If nobody owns the drawing, the carpenter becomes the last person blamed.
fieldNote: He has **never used AI** and prefers accountable drawings to learning an unproven tool.
The **apprentice** is his concrete concern; he expects to preserve his own pay and site role.

steps.text: Ask union site representative to raise drawing revisions at safety meeting
Keep fitting timber and require dated signed drawings before cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 could remake plans and buying in two years, while building robots able to do our hands-on work arrive around 2031. We should not let a computer's drawing override a real wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid carpentry hours once robots can fit and carry as well as us, but I cannot say which site would buy them first. Our savings buy time, yet the mortgage and two children mean I need a wage, not just a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union for paid training in site safety inspection, but I would enrol only if the employer funds the course and gives paid time. In the first year after 2028, I'd keep carpentry shifts, inspect AI plans against the built wall and apply to posted local site-inspector vacancies only if the wage covers our mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the years before our mortgage is smaller. I have options nearby, but a quick loss of hours would hurt even with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the course offer for paid hours and a real certificate, then compare it with local inspector adverts. A site-safety course alone does not put dinner on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would hear that I am keeping the carpentry wage while I test the other route. I would show the savings balance and the posted wages, not promise a job I have not been offered.

say: **AGI by 2028** would change construction plans first; capable building robots would follow around 2031.
I would demand **paid training** and accountable checks of AI drawings against real walls.
think: Robot building could cut my **carpentry hours** before the mortgage is smaller.
Our **savings** help, but an inspection move needs a real vacancy and bill-covering pay.
do: **Enrol** in site-safety inspection training only with employer funding and paid course time.
**Keep** carpentry shifts and check AI plans against built walls after 2028.
**Apply** to posted local site-inspector vacancies only if wages cover mortgage and school bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost hours, while nearby sites and savings leave some control.
S2.quote: A site-safety course alone does not put dinner on the table.
fieldNote: The **2028 plan change** affects a small part of his role; 2031 robots pose the larger wage risk.
He will take **inspection training** only with funding and paid time, then pursue a posted local job at adequate pay.

steps.text: Enrol in funded site-safety inspection course only with paid time
Keep carpentry shifts and check AI plans against built walls
Apply for posted local inspector jobs only at bill-covering wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2031 gives us five years to sort out drawings and about three more before capable building robots arrive around 2034. I want a negotiated route for tradespeople before any site cuts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to see whether inspection work really opens nearby, but I am not changing trades on a rumour. Our savings and the nearby building work make the first years manageable; the mortgage still needs proper wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the union to bargain for paid site-safety training places, and I would join a course only once funding and paid time are agreed. In the first year after 2031, I'd keep carpentry work and apply for a posted local inspector position if its pay covers the household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened for now. The extra years let me check a real offer instead of jumping at a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real inspector opening show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a posted salary, training requirement and site location. A far-away vacancy would not work with school pickup unless we changed the whole household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the union secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union should ask for paid course hours written into the agreement. I will not spend our family reserve on a course an employer says it needs.

say: **AGI by 2031** allows five years before plan work changes and until around 2034 before capable building robots.
I would seek a **negotiated route** into paid inspection work before hours are cut.
think: Nearby work and **strong savings** protect our household during the first years.
The **mortgage** means I still need bill-covering wages from any local inspector job.
do: **Ask** the union to bargain for funded inspection training with paid course hours.
**Enrol** only once the employer funds site-safety training and pays for attendance.
**Apply** after 2031 for a posted local inspector role only at bill-covering pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about future site changes, but the longer lead time lets me check real offers.
S3.quote: I will not spend our family reserve on a course an employer says it needs.
fieldNote: He rejects **speculative retraining**, yet would take a funded course during paid hours.
A **local posting** and a salary covering mortgage and school bills control any job move.

steps.text: Ask union to bargain for employer-funded inspection training and paid time
Enrol in funded site-safety course only with paid hours agreed in writing
Apply for posted local inspector job only at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives ten years before the office plans change and capable building robots come around 2039. We should use the time to protect the trade, not pretend the date will never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older and we may have paid down much of the mortgage by then, if work holds. I would still rather stay a carpenter than learn a new trade for a future nobody can pin down today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading carpentry crews and pay a little extra against the mortgage each month from our current higher wage. In the first year after 2036, I'd compare actual local site vacancies and wages before moving anywhere, while checking the AI plan against the work in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for our household finances over that runway. I am still protective of young tradespeople coming through after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a trainee to learn proper setting out and how to reject a bad drawing. A robot timetable is no excuse for a wall that is out of square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your present site slowed down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If local building work really fell, I would apply to a posted carpentry job at another nearby site only if the wage still paid the mortgage. I would not move the children on the strength of a forecast.

say: **AGI by 2036** leaves a decade before plan work changes and capable building robots follow around 2039.
I would keep teaching **setting out** and challenging bad drawings.
think: Our **mortgage** could be smaller by then if higher wages continue.
I prefer **carpentry** to an uncertain new trade and will judge local vacancies when they exist.
do: **Keep** leading carpentry crews and paying extra against the mortgage monthly.
**Check** AI plans against built walls after 2036 while still doing site work.
**Apply** to a posted nearby carpentry job only if current work falls and wages cover bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about our finances on a decade-long runway, though younger tradespeople stay on my mind.
S4.quote: A robot timetable is no excuse for a wall that is out of square.
fieldNote: He uses the **long runway** to reduce mortgage debt while staying in familiar carpentry.
A job application remains **conditional** on weaker local work, a real nearby posting and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Keep leading carpentry crews and checking built walls against plans
Pay extra against the mortgage monthly from current higher wages
Apply for posted nearby carpentry work only if current hours fall and pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because plans could change almost at once and robots around 2031 might cut my carpentry hours while the children and mortgage still need my wage. Employer-funded inspection training on paid time, a real local vacancy at bill-covering pay and a union safety agreement would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who can stop a bad cut after an AI drawing changes. A carpenter on the site needs the right to put down the saw without losing pay.

portrait: **Hassan**, forty-three, leads carpentry and general building work, with a trade certificate and a reputation for catching bad dimensions.
His **higher wage**, strong savings and many nearby sites support a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He **avoids new technology**, never uses AI tools and presses his union for accountable drawings and paid safety training.
The **2028** case threatens paid site hours earliest; longer cases give him time to protect income and pay down the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change site plans quickly and bring capable building robots around 2031, risking carpentry hours.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded training** during paid hours, a posted local inspector vacancy at bill-covering pay and a union safety agreement would help.
headlineQuote: A carpenter on the site needs the right to put down the saw without losing pay.
